(10.10.4) FJ​o​s​h​i⊢⁣▶​(X/Lv,Kv)\displaystyle{F}^{\vdash\blacktriangleright}_{\scriptscriptstyle{Joshi}}(X/L_{v};K_{v}) =GLv​↷​q(X/Lv,X/Kv)ℕ\displaystyle=G_{L_{v}}\overset{}{\curvearrowright}q_{(X/L_{v},X/K_{v})}^{\mathbb{N}}
(10.10.5) FJ​o​s​h​i⊢⁣⟂​(X/Lv,Kv)\displaystyle{F}^{\vdash\perp}_{\scriptscriptstyle{Joshi}}(X/L_{v};K_{v}) =GLv​↷​OL¯vμ2​ℓ×q(X/Lv,X/Kv)ℕ.\displaystyle=G_{L_{v}}\overset{}{\curvearrowright}{O}_{\overline{L}_{v}}^{\mu_{2\ell}}\times q_{(X/L_{v},X/K_{v})}^{\mathbb{N}}.

If 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​(Y/Lv,Kv,1)\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}(Y/L_{v};K_{v,1}) and 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​(X/Lv,Kv,2)\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}(X/L_{v};K_{v,2}) are two tempered frobenioids arising from two holomorphoids X/𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(𝐲1)X/\mathfrak{arith}({\bf y}_{1}) and X/𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(𝐲1)X/\mathfrak{arith}({\bf y}_{1}) then one has an isomorphism between the tempered fundamental groups

ΠX/Lv;Kv,1t​e​m​p≃ΠX/Lv;Kv,2t​e​m​p,\Pi^{\scriptscriptstyle temp}_{X/L_{v};K_{v,1}}\simeq\Pi^{\scriptscriptstyle temp}_{X/L_{v};K_{v,2}},

and an isomorphism

FJ​o​s​h​i?​(X/Lv,Kv,1)≃FJ​o​s​h​i?​(X/Lv,Kv,2){F}_{\scriptscriptstyle{Joshi}}^{?}(X/L_{v};K_{v,1})\simeq{F}_{\scriptscriptstyle{Joshi}}^{?}(X/L_{v};K_{v,2})

between each prime-strip, given in Section 8.5, corresponding to these two frobenioids.

Proof.

The proof is immediate from Theorem 8.8.3.

Remark.

One may view Theorems 10.10.1 and 8.8.3 as providing a “gluing” of the Frobenioids 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​(Y/Lv,Kv,1)\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}(Y/L_{v};K_{v,1}) and 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​(X/Lv,Kv,2)\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}(X/L_{v};K_{v,2}) and Hodge-Theaters (see § 10.11) by along their respective prime strips (see [Mochizuki, 2021a, § I2, page 21]). There are other instances of similar “gluing” assertions in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c]. ∙\bullet

§ 10.11 Mochizuki’s Hodge Theaters via [Joshi, 2021a]

Another device which is used in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c] is the notion of a Hodge-Theater which is introduced in [Mochizuki, 2021a]. Using Section 8.5, the discussion of tempered Frobenioids in § 10.9, and the theory of arithmeticoids [Joshi, 2023a], one can translate this notion into more transparent objects of [Joshi, 2021a]. Notably, this demonstrates the existence of a plurality of Hodge Theaters of all types considered in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c]. There are many different Hodge Theaters used in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c], with increasing complexity but built roughly on the same principles. I will provide the simplest version but let me remark that such devices are unnecessary in [Joshi, 2021a, Joshi, 2022, Joshi, 2023a] as more geometric objects are available.

§ 10.11.1 

Let L,C/L,X/L,L′,LmodL,C/L,X/L,L^{\prime},L_{\rm mod} be as in § 2.4, § 3.1, § 3.3. Let LmodL_{\rm mod} be the field of moduli of X/LX/L. So LmodL_{\rm mod} is the field of moduli of X/LX/L and explicitly LmodL_{\rm mod} is the field generated over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} by the jj-invariant of the projective elliptic curve giving rise to XX. So one has L⊃LmodL\supset L_{\rm mod}.

§ 10.11.2 

One has the adelic Arithmetic Teichmuller Space 𝔍⁡(X/L)~\widetilde{\mathfrak{J}(X/L)} constructed by [Joshi, 2021a, Theorem ]. This is a product of local arithmetic Teichmuller spaces 𝔍⁡(X,L𝔭)\mathfrak{J}(X,L_{\mathfrak{p}}) for all vv. At archimedean primes one takes the usual Teichmuller spaces associated to the Riemann surface X⁡(Lv)X(L_{v}) (here v=∞v=\infty and by hypothesis LL has no real embeddings).

By [Joshi, 2021a, Theorem ], for every prime vv of LL, every object of 𝔍arith​(X,Lv)\mathfrak{J}^{\rm arith}({X,L_{v}}) is definable over LmodL_{\rm mod}.

§ 10.11.3 

Suppose that one is given a point ((X/Lv,X/Kv)v)∈𝔍⁡(X/L)~((X/L_{v},X/K_{v})_{v})\in\widetilde{\mathfrak{J}(X/L)} of the adelic arithmetic Teichmuller space 𝔍⁡(X/L)~\widetilde{\mathfrak{J}(X/L)} constructed in [Joshi, 2021a]. Then by [Joshi, 2023a, Proposition ] one obtains an arithmeticoid 𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(L)𝐲\mathfrak{arith}(L)_{\bf y} associated to ((X/Lv,X/Kv)v∈𝕍L)∈𝔍⁡(X/L)~((X/L_{v},X/K_{v})_{v\in\mathbb{V}_{L}})\in\widetilde{\mathfrak{J}(X/L)}.

Theorem 10.11.3.1.

Let C,X,L,L′C,X,L,L^{\prime} be as in § 2.4 and § 3.1, § 3.3. Let ((X/Lv′,X/Kv)v∈𝕍L′)∈𝔍⁡(X/L)~∈𝔍⁡(X/L)((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v})_{v\in\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}}})\in\widetilde{\mathfrak{J}(X/L)}\in\mathfrak{J}(X/L) be a point of the adelic Teichmuller space of X/LX/L and 𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(L′)𝐲\mathfrak{arith}(L^{\prime})_{\bf y} be the arithmeticoid of L′L^{\prime} provided by this point. Then

  1. (1)

    the bijection (see § 3.1, § 3.3)

    𝕍Lmod≃𝕍¯⊂𝕍L′\mathbb{V}_{L_{\rm mod}}\simeq\underline{\mathbb{V}}\subset\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}}

    together with the arithmeticoid 𝐲{\bf y} provides us with an arithmeticoid 𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}} with 𝐲¯∈𝐘𝐋mod{\underline{{\bf y}}}\in\mathscrbf{Y}_{L_{\rm mod}} naturally given using 𝐲{\bf y} and the above bijection.

  2. (2)

    In particular, every holomorphoid 𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L′)𝐲\mathfrak{hol}(X/L^{\prime})_{{\bf y}} of X/L′X/L^{\prime} provides us an arithmeticoid

    𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}}

    of LmodL_{\rm mod},

  3. (3)

    and hence by [Joshi, 2023a, Proposition ] a (perfect) frobenioid

    𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯),\mathfrak{Frob}(\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}}),

    and a realified Frobenioid

    𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯)ℝ\mathfrak{Frob}(\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}})^{\mathbb{R}}

    which are isomorphic (by [Joshi, 2023a, Proposition ]) to the perfection 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(Lmod)p​f\mathfrak{Frob}(L_{\rm mod})^{pf} and the realification 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(Lmod)ℝ\mathfrak{Frob}(L_{\rm mod})^{{\mathbb{R}}} of the Frobenioid of the number field LmodL_{\rm mod} respectively.

Proof.

To prove all the assertions, it is enough to provide a natural construction of 𝐲¯∈𝐘𝐋mod\underline{{\bf y}}\in\mathscrbf{Y}_{L_{\rm mod}} from 𝐲∈𝐘𝐋′{\bf y}\in\mathscrbf{Y}_{L^{\prime}} given by the data of the holomorphoid 𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L)𝐲\mathfrak{hol}(X/L)_{{\bf y}} and the bijection 𝕍Lmod≃𝕍¯⊂𝕍L′\mathbb{V}_{L_{\rm mod}}\simeq\underline{\mathbb{V}}\subset\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}} provided by § 3.1, § 3.3. By definition ([Joshi, 2023a, Definition ]) that

𝐘𝐋′=∏𝐰∈𝕍𝐋′|𝐘ℂ𝐩♭,𝐋𝐰′|.\mathscrbf{Y}_{L^{\prime}}=\prod_{w\in\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}}}\left|{Y}_{{\mathbb{C}}_{p}^{\flat},L_{w}^{\prime}}\right|.

Now 𝐲¯∈𝐘𝐋mod\underline{{\bf y}}\in\mathscrbf{Y}_{L_{\rm mod}} is the point obtained by projection of 𝐲=(yw′)w∈𝕍L′{\bf y}=(y^{\prime}_{w})_{w\in\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}}} on to the coordinates corresponding to the “index” set identified by 𝕍¯≃𝕍Lmod\underline{\mathbb{V}}\simeq\mathbb{V}_{L_{\rm mod}} using the natural (continuous) mapping [Fargues and Fontaine, 2018, Proposition 2.3.20]

fw|v:|Yℂp♭,Lw′|→|Yℂp♭,Lmod,v|f_{w|v}:\left|{Y}_{{\mathbb{C}}_{p}^{\flat},L_{w}^{\prime}}\right|\to\left|{Y}_{{\mathbb{C}}_{p}^{\flat},{L_{\rm mod}}_{,v}}\right|

i.e. define

𝐲¯=(fw|v​(yw′))w∈𝕍¯∈𝐘𝐋mod′.\underline{{\bf y}}=(f_{w|v}(y_{w}^{\prime}))_{w\in\underline{\mathbb{V}}}\in\mathscrbf{Y}_{L_{\rm mod}}^{\prime}.

§ 10.11.4 

For each holomorphoid 𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L′)𝐲\mathfrak{hol}(X/L^{\prime})_{{\bf y}} and for each v∈𝕍L′v\in\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}}, let (X/Lv′,X/Kv)=𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/Lv′)yv(X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v})=\mathfrak{hol}(X/L_{v}^{\prime})_{y_{v}} be the (local) holomorphoid of X/Lv′X/L_{v}^{\prime}. Let 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​((X/Lv′,X/Kv))yv\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v}))_{y_{v}} be the tempered Frobenioid of X/LvX/L_{v} at vv associated to it by § 10.9, [Joshi, 2023a, Definition ].

Let 𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}} be the arithmeticoid of LmodL_{\rm mod} given by Theorem 10.11.3.1. Let 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯)\mathfrak{Frob}(\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}}) (resp. 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯)ℝ\mathfrak{Frob}(\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}})^{\mathbb{R}}) be the Frobenioid (resp. the realified Frobenioid) associated to the arithmeticoid 𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{{\bf y}}} by [Joshi, 2023a, Proposition ]. Let 𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(Lmod)ℝ\mathfrak{Frob}(L_{\rm mod})^{\mathbb{R}} be the realification of the Frobenioid of the number field LmodL_{\rm mod} (see § 10.5).

Then one can associate to 𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L′)𝐲\mathfrak{hol}(X/L^{\prime})_{{\bf y}}, a Hodge Theater, in the sense of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Definition 3.6], as follows:

(10.11.4.1) ℋ​𝒯​((X/Lv′,X/Kv)v)𝐲=({𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​((X/Lv′,X/Kv))}v,𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(Lmod)𝐲¯¯)ℝ).\mathcal{HT}((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v})_{v})_{{\bf y}}=\left(\left\{\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v}))\right\}_{v},\mathfrak{Frob}(\mathfrak{arith}(L_{\rm mod})_{\underline{\underline{{\bf y}}}})^{\mathbb{R}}\right).

I will simply write this Hodge-Theater as

ℋ​𝒯​(𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L′)𝐲¯)\mathcal{HT}(\mathfrak{hol}(X/L^{\prime})_{\underline{{\bf y}}})

or even more simply as

ℋ​𝒯​(𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L))𝐲¯\mathcal{HT}(\mathfrak{hol}(X/L))_{\underline{{\bf y}}}

to indicate the holomorphoid of X/𝔞​𝔯​𝔦​𝔱​𝔥​(L′)𝐲X/\mathfrak{arith}(L^{\prime})_{\bf y} which it arises from.

By [Joshi, 2023a, Proposition ] one may also write the above definition in the style of [Mochizuki, 2021a] as

(10.11.4.2) ℋ​𝒯​((X/Lv′,X/Kv)v)𝐲=({𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​((X/Lv′,X/Kv))}v∈𝕍L′,𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟​(Lmod)𝐲¯ℝ).\mathcal{HT}((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v})_{v})_{{\bf y}}=\left(\left\{\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v}))\right\}_{v\in\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}}},\mathfrak{Frob}({L_{\rm mod}})^{\mathbb{R}}_{\underline{{\bf y}}}\right).
Remark 10.11.4.3.

Notably, Hodge Theaters in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c] should be labeled by the arithmetic holomorphic structures they arise from. ∙\bullet

§ 10.11.5 

This is an important point for [Mochizuki, 2021c]:

Theorem 10.11.5.1.

Each holomorphoid 𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L)𝐲\mathfrak{hol}(X/L)_{{\bf y}} provides the Hodge-Theater

ℋ​𝒯​(𝔥​𝔬​𝔩​(X/L′))𝐲\mathcal{HT}(\mathfrak{hol}(X/L^{\prime}))_{{\bf y}}

and all these distinct holomorphoids give rise to isomorphic Hodge Theaters.

Proof.

Note that by the theory of [Joshi, 2021a, Joshi, 2022, Joshi, 2023b] there are many inequivalent geometric data indexed by 𝐲∈𝐘𝐋′′{\bf y}\in\mathscrbf{Y}_{L^{\prime}}^{\prime} and each provides the corresponding Hodge-Theater

ℋ​𝒯​((X/Lv′,X/Kv)v)=({𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟t​e​m​p​((X/Lv′,X/Kv))}v,𝔉​𝔯​𝔬​𝔟ℝ​(Lmod)).\mathcal{HT}((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v})_{v})=\left(\{\mathfrak{Frob}_{temp}((X/L^{\prime}_{v},X/K_{v}))\}_{v},\mathfrak{Frob}^{\mathbb{R}}(L_{\rm mod})\right).

To prove all these Hodge-Theaters are isomorphic, it suffices to note that each arises from the data of tempered coverings of X/Lv′X/L_{v}^{\prime} and the monoid of effective divisors and principal divisors on each of these coverings. Assume that v∈𝕍L′v\in\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}} is non-archimedean. By [André, 2003b], these tempered coverings of X/Lv′X/L_{v}^{\prime} are defined over finite extensions of Lv′L_{v}^{\prime} contained in KvK_{v}. For vv archimedean, a tempered covering is by definition a finite étale covering and hence such a covering is defined over a finite extension of L′L^{\prime}. So for all v∈𝕍L′v\in\mathbb{V}_{L^{\prime}}, one has a non-canonical isomorphism between such data provided by any two holomorphoids. Hence the assertion is established.

Remark 10.11.5.2.
  1. (1)

    Mochizuki defines other versions of Hodge Theaters ℋ​𝒯?\mathcal{HT}^{?} with more refined conditions and decorations, but I will not recall these here.

  2. (2)

    Hodge Theaters of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c] consist of data coarser than the geometric data of [Joshi, 2021a, Joshi, 2022, Joshi, 2023a]. All Hodge Theaters of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c] can be easily constructed by using the above methods and the present series of papers ([Joshi, 2021a, Joshi, 2022, Joshi, 2023b, Joshi, 2023a] and this paper).

  3. (3)

    The above proposition should be contrasted with [Scholze, 2021]. The central point which is missing in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c] (and in [Scholze, 2021]) is the existence of geometrically inequivalent data providing the above Hodge-Theaters.

  4. (4)

    Readers of [Scholze, 2021] may have drawn the (erroneous) conclusion that the equivalence of Hodge-Theaters invalidates the methodology and the claims of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c].

  5. (5)

    So let me say this clearly: [Mochizuki, 2021c, Corollary 3.12] is not about Hodge-Theaters or fundamental groups per se, but about averaging arithmetic and geometric data arising from distinct arithmetic holomorphic structures. That distinct arithmetic holomorphic structures exist and that such an averaging is possible is asserted in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c] and unequivocally established in the present series of papers ([Joshi, 2021a, Joshi, 2022, Joshi, 2023b, Joshi, 2023a] and this paper).

∙\bullet

11 Appendix II: Perfect Frobenioids vs. Perfectoids

In this section, I want to provide a comparison between the theory of perfect Frobenioids and the theory of perfectoids. Mochizuki’s Frobenioid theoretic (read multiplicative monoid theoretic) approach requires decoupling addition and multiplication in the sense of this paper. Mochizuki asserts that this decoupling is possible by his group theoretic methods. As noted in [Joshi, 2023a, § ], in [Joshi, 2019], I showed that one may also establish this decoupling algebraically keeping Mochizuki’s monoid theoretic ideas as a guide; an important observation I made early on is that the theory of perfectoid spaces of [Scholze, 2012] also provides such a decoupling (as observed in this paper) via existence of general Fargues-Fontaine curves after [Kedlaya and Liu, 2015, Kedlaya and Liu, 2019] and [Scholze, 2012, Scholze and Weinstein, 2020].

§ 11.1 A useful multiplicative sheaf

The following will be useful in what follows:

Proposition 11.1.1.

Let X/kX/k be a geometrically connected, smooth, quasi-projective variety over a field kk. For each n∈ℤ≥0n\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}, let ϕn:OX∗→OX∗\phi_{n}:{O}_{X}^{*}\to{O}_{X}^{*} be the homomorphism of sheaves of abelian groups given by x⟼xn{x\longmapsto x^{n}}. Consider the (inverse) limit presheaf

OX∗p​f=lim←n⁡(OX∗,ϕn).{O}_{X}^{*pf}=\varprojlim_{n}({O}_{X}^{*},\phi_{n}).

Then OX∗p​f{O}_{X}^{*pf} is a sheaf of abelian groups whose sections over open subsets (and hence also stalks) are perfect monoids in the sense of [Mochizuki, 2008]. Notably the stalks of OX∗p​f{O}_{X}^{*pf} are perfect monoids i.e. the stalks are ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-vector spaces.

Proof.

This is immediate from the well-known fact that limits of sheaves of abelian groups (on quasi-projective or more generally noetherian schemes) are sheaves.

Along with (X,OX∗p​f)(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf}) may similarly consider the pair (X,(OX,+)p​f)(X,({O}_{X},+)^{pf}) with

(OX,+)p​f=lim←n⁡(OX,+),({O}_{X},+)^{pf}=\varprojlim_{n}({O}_{X},+),

where the inverse limit is over the homomorphism OX→OX{O}_{X}\to{O}_{X} of abelian groups given by x⟼n⋅xx\longmapsto n\cdot x for local sections xx of OX{O}_{X}. The sheaf of abelian groups (OX,+)p​f({O}_{X},+)^{pf} is a sheaf of perfect monoids in the sense of [Mochizuki, 2008].

More generally, suppose X/kX/k is an integral scheme, and let KX∗K_{X}^{*} be the sheaf of invertible, meromorphic functions on XX, the one may also consider (X,KX∗p​f)(X,K_{X}^{*pf}) instead.

Remark 11.1.2.

Notably the pairs (X,OX∗p​f)(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf}) (resp. (X,OX∗p​f)(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf})) consisting of the topological space XX equipped with the perfect multiplicative monoid (perfect additive monoid) (both are sheaves of abelian groups in fact) of functions on XX exists even if XX does not admit a perfectoidification in the sense of [Scholze, 2012]. ∙\bullet

§ 11.2 Multiplicatoids

Now let me explain how one may decouple additive and multiplicative structures. Instead of working with the scheme structure (X,OX)(X,{O}_{X}), one can work with the pair (X,OX∗p​f)(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf}). I call (X,OX∗p​f)(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf}) the perfect multiplicatoid of the scheme (X,OX)(X,{O}_{X}). Similarly, one calls the pair (X,(OX,+)p​f)(X,({O}_{X},+)^{pf}), the additivoid of XX.

One may think of the (X,OX∗p​f)(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf}) and (X,(OX,+)p​f)(X,({O}_{X},+)^{pf}) as a decoupling of the multiplication and addition structures of the scheme (X,OX)(X,{O}_{X}).

Remark 11.2.1.

Simplest example of this is the case when X=Spec⁡(L¯)X={\rm Spec}(\overline{L}) where L¯\overline{L} is the algebraic closure of a number field LL. The case of the multiplicatoid (|Spec⁡(L¯)|,L¯∗p​f)(\left|{\rm Spec}(\overline{L})\right|,\overline{L}^{*pf}) (here |Spec⁡(L)|\left|{\rm Spec}(L)\right| is the topological space underlying XX, this of course, a one point topological space) is implicitly considered in [Mochizuki, 2008] and importantly in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d]. Similarly, if pp is a prime, then the multplicatoid (|Spec⁡(ℚ¯p)|,ℚ¯p∗p​f)(\left|{\rm Spec}({\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}}_{p})\right|,{\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}}_{p}^{*pf}) of Spec⁡(ℚ¯p){\rm Spec}({\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}}_{p}) is of fundamental importance in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d]. ∙\bullet

§ 11.3 A basic problem

An important question which comes up in the context of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d] is this: Given the multiplicatoid of XX, recover or reconstruct some scheme structure on XX compatible with this multiplicative structure given by the multiplicatoid on XX.

More precisely, consider the problem of finding schemes (Y,OY)(Y,{O}_{Y}) with isomorphisms between their multiplicatoids

(11.3.1) (Y,OY∗p​f)≃(X,OX∗p​f).(Y,{O}_{Y}^{*pf})\simeq(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf}).

More generally, if MX⊆KX∗p​fM_{X}\subseteq K_{X}^{*pf} some suitably chosen subsheaf of monoids of the perfection of the sheaf, KX∗K_{X}^{*}, of invertible functions on XX, then one may consider the same question with (X,MX)(X,M_{X}) in place of (X,OX∗p​f)(X,{O}_{X}^{*pf}).

This is the precise version of the idea behind Mochizuki’s decoupling of addition and multiplication and reconstruction of a new scheme structure, namely (Y,OY)(Y,{O}_{Y}), from the multiplicatoid of XX. This point is of course not clearly enunciated in [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d] or in [Mochizuki, 2022] and nor is the mechanism for such a claim established.

§ 11.4 How do multiplicatoids arise in the anabelian contexts?

To understand how multiplicatoids arise naturally in anabelian contexts, let me present a reformulation of the classical anabelian reconstruction results for number fields and pp-adic fields ([Hoshi, 2015], [Hoshi, 2021] are great modern references for this):

Theorem 11.4.1.

Let kk be either a number field or a pp-adic field for some prime pp and let k¯\bar{k} be an algebraic closure of kk and let GkG_{k} be the absolute galois group of kk computed using k¯\bar{k}. Then from the topological GkG_{k} one can reconstruct some isomorph of the multiplicatoid (|Spec⁡(k¯)|,k¯∗p​f)(\left|{\rm Spec}(\bar{k})\right|,\bar{k}^{*pf}) of k¯\bar{k} and this reconstruction is functorial in kk. In other words, (|Spec⁡(k¯)|,k¯∗p​f)(\left|{\rm Spec}(\bar{k})\right|,\bar{k}^{*pf}) is amphoric.

§ 11.5 

In [Joshi, 2019], I showed that one may in fact algebraize the idea of decoupling of the additive and multiplicative structures by means of monoid formal group laws and universal monoid formal group law established in [Joshi, 2019] (a precise version of this relevant to the main results of this paper is recorded in [Joshi, 2023a, Theorem ]).

§ 11.6 

My first important observation is that the existence of distinct schemes (Y,OY)(Y,{O}_{Y}) in (11.3.1) is difficult to establish convincingly if one works with the category of schemes (as Mochizuki does). This difficulty already appears in the special case of of a geometric schematic point X=Spec⁡(ℚ¯p)X={\rm Spec}({\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}}_{p}) which is relevant to [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d]. For [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d], one needs a precise quantification of what “some” means in the above theorem.

§ 11.7 Multiplicatoids from perfectoid spaces

My second important observation is that Scholze’s work [Scholze, 2012] provides solution to a similar problem in a manner compatible with Mochizuki’s anabelian view point. Here is precise formulation:

Theorem 11.7.1.

Let (X,OX)(X,{O}_{X}) is a perfectoid space (for simplicity, one may assume that XX arises from a perfectoid algebra) over an algebraically closed perfectoid field. Suppose that (X♭,OX♭)(X^{\flat},{O}_{X^{\flat}}) is the tilt of (X,OX)(X,{O}_{X}). Let (Y,OY)(Y,{O}_{Y}) be another untilt of (X♭,OX♭)(X^{\flat},{O}_{X^{\flat}}) then

  1. (1)

    one has a homeomorphism of pairs consisting of a topological space and a sheaf of pp-perfect multiplicative monoids

    (11.7.2) (|Y|,lim←x⟼xp⁡OY)≃(|X|,lim←x⟼xp⁡OX).(\left|Y\right|,\varprojlim_{x\longmapsto x^{p}}{O}_{Y})\simeq(\left|X\right|,\varprojlim_{x\longmapsto x^{p}}{O}_{X}).
  2. (2)

    and there exists pairs (X,OX)(X,{O}_{X}) of perfectoid spaces which are not isomorphic, but for which the above isomorphism holds.

  3. (3)

    Moreover, for a suitable choice of geometric basepoints, one has an isomorphism of étale fundamental groups

    (11.7.3) π1e​t​(X)≃π1e​t​(Y).\pi_{1}^{et}(X)\simeq\pi_{1}^{et}(Y).

Proof.

By [Scholze, 2012, Theorem 1.8] one has an isomorphism of sheaves of topological rings (and hence of their subsheaves of multiplicative monoids)

(11.7.4) OX♭=lim←x⟼xp⁡OX,{O}_{X^{\flat}}=\varprojlim_{x\longmapsto x^{p}}{O}_{X},

and by [Scholze, 2012, Theorem 6.2] one has a homeomorphism of topological spaces

(11.7.5) |X|≃|X♭|.\left|X\right|\simeq\left|X^{\flat}\right|.

Thus one obtains an isomorphism of pairs for X,X♭X,X^{\flat}

(11.7.6) (|X♭|,OX♭)≃(|X|,lim←x⟼xp⁡OX).(\left|X^{\flat}\right|,{O}_{X^{\flat}})\simeq(\left|X\right|,\varprojlim_{x\longmapsto x^{p}}{O}_{X}).

In particular, the isomorphism class of the pair for XX depends only on X♭X^{\flat}. Hence if (X,OX),(Y,OY)(X,{O}_{X}),(Y,{O}_{Y}) are two untilts of (X♭,OX♭)(X^{\flat},{O}_{X^{\flat}}) then one has an isomorphism of the stated pairs. This proves (1).

In general the two perfectoid spaces with isomorphic tilts need not be isomorphic. An explicit example of this is provided, in the case XX arises from a perfectoid field, by the main theorem of [Kedlaya and Temkin, 2018]. This proves (2).

Now suppose one chooses geometric basepoints for X,X♭X,X^{\flat} then [Scholze, 2012, Theorem 7.12] shows that one has an isomorphism of étale fundamental groups of XX and X♭X^{\flat}, and hence the isomorphism class of this group depends only on that of X♭X^{\flat}. This proves (3).

§ 11.8 Comparison

Remark 11.8.1.
  1. (1)

    So one has a non-trivial solutions to the above problem in the category of perfectoid spaces.

  2. (2)

    Hence for a perfectoid space XX over an algebraically closed perfectoid field, the sheaf OX♭=lim←x⟼xp⁡OX{O}_{X^{\flat}}=\varprojlim_{x\longmapsto x^{p}}{O}_{X} plays a role similar to the sheaf encapsulating the multiplicatoid of a scheme considered above.

∙\bullet

Remark 11.8.2.

My approach to the aforementioned problem, developed in the present series of papers, is to work with Berkovich analytic spaces. This has an added advantage which is not available in the category of schemes: in category of Berkovich analytic spaces, generally speaking, logarithms of invertible functions are available and one can recover the additive structure of functions (i.e. recover the sheaf of abelian groups (OX,+)({O}_{X},+)–or some subsheaf thereof) from the multiplicative datum OX∗p​f{O}_{X}^{*pf} by passage to logarithms of suitably invertible functions i.e. one may treat the additive and multiplicative structure as being interchangeable. ∙\bullet

Remark 11.8.3.

Now to compare the two notions: the theory of perfect Frobenioids or more precisely perfect multiplicatoids is available for any geometrically connected smooth hyperbolic curve over a pp-adic field (and more generally for any smooth variety over a pp-adic field). More precisely the perfect multiplicatoid (11.3.1) exists for any scheme XX. But as has been remarked in [Scholze, 2014], the ‘perfectoidification’ of a hyperbolic curve does not exist (even for hyperbolic curves over algebraically closed perfectoid fields).

Hence, the theory of pairs (11.3.1) implicit in [Mochizuki, 2008] is at once more general but at the same time weaker than the theory of perfectoid spaces of [Scholze, 2012]. ∙\bullet

12 Appendix III: The proof of geometric Szpiro inequality revisited

§ 12.1 The proofs of geometric Szpiro inequality

In [Amorós et al., 2000], the authors gave a proof of geometric Szpiro inequality for elliptic fibrations over a genus zero curve and in [Zhang, 2001] this was generalized to elliptic fibrations over base curves of genus g≥0g\geq 0. In Spring 2018, I was on a sabbatical to RIMS, Kyoto with Shinichi Mochizuki and he gave me a few private lectures on his approach ( [Mochizuki, 2016]) to these works. As Mochizuki informs us in [Mochizuki, 2016], Ivan Fesenko had pointed out to him the existence of [Amorós et al., 2000], [Zhang, 2001].

Note that [Amorós et al., 2000], [Zhang, 2001] and [Mochizuki, 2016] deal with the same theorem (namely the geometric Szpiro inequality) from three different perspectives.

Here I will record a fourth distinct approach to understanding these three approaches to geometric Szpiro inequality which I discovered in the course of my work on arithmetic Teichmuller spaces. Notably the perspective presented below exhibits all the key features of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d], and also the perspective of this paper and a reading of this is essential for anyone who wishes to understand [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d], my work and the relationship between these two theories. In particular, I provide a formulation (and a proof) of [Mochizuki, 2021c, Corollary 3.12] in the context of the geometric Szpiro inequality (this is not formulated in [Mochizuki, 2016]).

This section should be read in tandem with [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000]. ([Mochizuki, 2016] largely follows these references with added commentary).

§ 12.2 The setup

Let CC be a connected, smooth, projective curve over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} of genus g≥0g\geq 0. Let f:X→Cf:X\to C be a proper, generically smooth morphism with geometric generic fiber of genus one. This fibration will be fixed for the remainder of this paper. Additionally I will assume that this is not an isotrivial fibration.

§ 12.3 The universal cover of SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) and its properties

Let SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) be the topological group of 2×22\times 2 matrices with real entries and of determinant one. Let SL2​(ℝ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} be the universal cover of SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}). Then SL2​(ℝ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} is described as a central extension ([Zhang, 2001, Lemma 3.5])

(12.3.1) 1→⟨z2⟩→SL2​(ℝ)~→SL2​(ℝ)→11\to\langle z^{2}\rangle\to\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}\to{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\to 1

where z∈SL2​(ℝ)~z\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} is a certain element, which generates the center of SL2​(ℝ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} and which is described explicitly in [Zhang, 2001] and so I will not recall that description here.

Let

SL2​(ℤ)~⊂SL2​(ℝ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}})}\subset\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}

be the inverse image of SL2​(ℤ)⊂SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}})\subset{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}). Let

SL2​(ℚ)~⊂SL2​(ℝ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}\subset\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}

be the inverse image of SL2​(ℚ)⊂SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})\subset{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}).

Remark 12.3.2.

Note that by classical results or the explicit description in [Amorós et al., 2000] or [Zhang, 2001], SL2​(ℤ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}})} is isomorphic to the braid group on three letters (see [Rawnsley, 2012, Theorem 16]). ∙\bullet

§ 12.4 Classical Teichmuller space in genus one

Let ℌ\mathfrak{H} be the complex upper half plane. Then one has a natural mapping

SL2​(ℝ)→ℌ{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\to\mathfrak{H}

given by

[abcd]⟼a⋅i+bc⋅i+d.\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{bmatrix}\longmapsto\frac{a\cdot i+b}{c\cdot i+d}.

If τ∈ℌ\tau\in\mathfrak{H}, I will write EτE_{\tau} for the elliptic curve given by the lattice [1,τ]⊂ℂ[1,\tau]\subset{\mathbb{C}}.

Recall from [Imayoshi and Taniguchi, 1992] that ℌ\mathfrak{H} is the Teichmuller space of genus one Riemann surfaces and the usual modular group SL2​(ℤ)⊂SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}})\subset{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) can be identified with the Teichmuller modular group (in genus one).

§ 12.5 Global (geometric) Fargues-Fontaine curves Y∞{Y}_{\infty}, X∞{X}_{\infty}, and the global Frobenius morphism φ∞\varphi_{\infty}

Let me now illustrate how the geometric analogues of 𝐘𝐋\mathscrbf{Y}_{L} i.e. global Fargues-Fontaine curve type objects with a similar geometry appears in the context of [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000]. This is an important point in understanding my approach and Mochizuki’s approach to global Diophantine problems via our respective theories.

Definition 12.5.1.

Let Y∞=SL2​(ℝ)~{Y}_{\infty}=\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} and X∞=SL2​(ℝ){X}_{\infty}={\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}). I will refer to Y∞{Y}_{\infty} as the incomplete global Fargues-Fontaine curve and X∞=SL2​(ℝ){X}_{\infty}={\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) as the complete global Fargues-Fontaine curve. I will write

(12.5.2) φ∞=z2∈SL2​(ℝ)~\varphi_{\infty}=z^{2}\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}

for the generator of the central extension (12.3.1) and refer to φ∞\varphi_{\infty} as the global Frobenius morphism of Y∞{Y}_{\infty}. In particular, with these definitions, and because of (12.3.1), one has

    with φ\varphi the Frobenius morphism of YF,E{Y}_{F,E}.

    Note however that the usual Fargues-Fontaine curve YF,E,XF,E{Y}_{F,E},{X}_{F,E} are local objects from the the point of view of theory of the present series of papers, while Y∞,X∞{Y}_{\infty},{X}_{\infty} are global objects in the context of [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000].

  4. (4)

    There is also an alternate global analog in the present theory: 𝐘𝐋\mathscrbf{Y}_{L} and the quotient (topological stack) [𝐘𝐋/𝐋∗][\mathscrbf{Y}_{L}/L^{*}] are also global analogs of Y∞,X∞{Y}_{\infty},{X}_{\infty} in the context of the present series of papers (and hence in the context of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d]).

∙\bullet

§ 12.6 Existence of 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links

In [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d] Mochizuki works with 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links. Let me discuss how this appears in the context of [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000]. Let gτ∈SL2​(ℝ)g_{\tau}\in{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) be a lift of τ∈ℌ\tau\in\mathfrak{H} to SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}). Let g~τ∈SL2​(ℝ)~\tilde{g}_{\tau}\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} be the lift of gτg_{\tau} to SL2​(ℝ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}.

Definition 12.6.1.

Let g~τ,0∈SL2​(ℝ)~\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} be a lift of τ∈ℌ\tau\in\mathfrak{H} to SL2​(ℝ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}. If g~τ,0′\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0} is another lift of τ\tau then I will say that g~τ,0\tilde{g}_{\tau,0} and g~τ,0′\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}^{\prime} are 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-linked if

g~τ,0′=g~τ,0⋅φ∞.\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0}=\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}\cdot\varphi_{\infty}.

I will call

{g~τ,n=g~τ,0⋅φ∞n:n∈ℤ}\left\{\tilde{g}_{\tau,n}=\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}\cdot\varphi_{\infty}^{n}:n\in{\mathbb{Z}}\right\}

a chain of 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links. ∙\bullet

Remark 12.6.2.

Note that a chain of 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links is the fiber over Y∞→X∞{Y}_{\infty}\to{X}_{\infty} over the common image of g~τ,n\tilde{g}_{\tau,n} in X∞=SL2​(ℝ){X}_{\infty}={\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}). ∙\bullet

§ 12.7 The Schottky parameter

Let me begin with the following

Lemma 12.7.1.

Let τ∈ℌ\tau\in\mathfrak{H}. For any α∈ℚ>0\alpha\in{\mathbb{Q}}^{>0}, the elliptic curves E1=ℂ/Λ1E_{1}={\mathbb{C}}/\Lambda_{1} and Eτ,α=ℂ/Λτ,αE_{\tau,\alpha}={\mathbb{C}}/\Lambda_{\tau,\alpha} given by the lattices Λτ,1=[1,τ]⊂ℂ\Lambda_{\tau,1}=[1,\tau]\subset{\mathbb{C}} and Λτ,α=[1,α⋅τ]\Lambda_{\tau,\alpha}=[1,\alpha\cdot\tau] are ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-isogenous.

It is sufficient to note that (100α)∈GL2+​(ℚ)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&\alpha\end{pmatrix}\in{\rm GL}_{2}^{+}({\mathbb{Q}}) and

(100α)⋅(1τ)=(1α⋅τ)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&\alpha\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \tau\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \alpha\cdot\tau\end{pmatrix}

takes Λ1\Lambda_{1} to Λα\Lambda_{\alpha}. So the assertion is clear.

Definition 12.7.2.

For an elliptic curve EE given by a lattice [1,τ]⊂ℂ[1,\tau]\subset{\mathbb{C}} let qE=e2​π⋅−1​τq_{E}=e^{2\pi\cdot\sqrt{-1}\tau} be its Schottky parameter. Then one has the Schottky uniformization

E≃ℂ∗/qEℤ.E\simeq{\mathbb{C}}^{*}/q_{E}^{\mathbb{Z}}.

∙\bullet

Proof.

This is standard.

Lemma 12.7.3.

For the elliptic curves E1E_{1} and Eτ,αE_{\tau,\alpha} one has the following relationship between their Schottky parameters:

qEτ,α=qE1α.q_{E_{\tau,\alpha}}=q_{E_{1}}^{\alpha}.

This is an elementary calculation:

qEτ,α=e2​π⋅−1​(α⋅τ)=e2​π⋅−1⋅α⋅τ=qE1α.q_{E_{\tau,\alpha}}=e^{2\pi\cdot\sqrt{-1}(\alpha\cdot\tau)}=e^{2\pi\cdot\sqrt{-1}\cdot\alpha\cdot\tau}=q_{E_{1}}^{\alpha}.

§ 12.8 Existence of Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-links

Now I want to discuss how Mochizuki’s Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-link appears in the geometric case of [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000]. Let ℓ≥5\ell\geq 5 be a prime number, let ℓ∗=ℓ−12{\ell^{*}}=\frac{\ell-1}{2}. Let τ∈ℌ\tau\in\mathfrak{H} and write q=e2​π​−1​τq=e^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}\tau}. From now on, for j=1,2,…,ℓ∗j=1,2,\ldots,{\ell^{*}}, for simplicity of notation, I will write

Eτ,j=Eτ2​ℓ,j2.E_{\tau,j}=E_{\frac{\tau}{2\ell},j^{2}}.

Note that the lattice [1,τ⋅j22​ℓ][1,\frac{\tau\cdot j^{2}}{2\ell}] for Eτ,jE_{\tau,j} can be obtained from the lattice [1,τ2​ℓ][1,\frac{\tau}{2\ell}] of Eτ,1E_{\tau,1} by using the matrix

(j001j)∈SL2​(ℚ)\begin{pmatrix}j&0\\ 0&\frac{1}{j}\end{pmatrix}\in{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})

which takes operates on ℌ\mathfrak{H} by

τ⟼(j001j)⋅τ=j⋅τj−1=j2⋅τ,\tau\longmapsto\begin{pmatrix}j&0\\ 0&\frac{1}{j}\end{pmatrix}\cdot\tau=\frac{j\cdot\tau}{j^{-1}}={j^{2}\cdot\tau},

and hence τ2​ℓ⟼j2⋅τ2​ℓ\frac{\tau}{2\ell}\longmapsto\frac{j^{2}\cdot\tau}{2\ell} under its action.

The reason I want to consider SL2​(ℚ){\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}}) in place of GL2+​(ℚ){\rm GL}_{2}^{+}({\mathbb{Q}}) is that SL2​(ℚ)⊂SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})\subset{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}). Working with GL2+​(ℚ){\rm GL}_{2}^{+}({\mathbb{Q}}) would require replacing SL2​(ℝ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) by GL2+​(ℝ){\rm GL}_{2}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) in [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000]–this can be done, but presently I have not written down all the changes this necessitates in [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000]. ∙\bullet

Lemma 12.8.2.

Let

αj=(j001j)​ for ​j=1,2,…,ℓ∗.\alpha_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}j&0\\ 0&\frac{1}{j}\end{pmatrix}\text{ for }j=1,2,\ldots,{\ell^{*}}.

Then the ℓ∗{\ell^{*}}-tuple (α1,…,αℓ∗)∈SL2​(ℚ)ℓ∗(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{\ell^{*}})\in{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})^{\ell^{*}} operates on ℌℓ∗\mathfrak{H}^{\ell^{*}}, by the usual Mobius action on each of the factors, and under this action the diagonal tuple

(τ,τ,…,τ)∈ℌℓ∗(\tau,\tau,\ldots,\tau)\in\mathfrak{H}^{\ell^{*}}

is mapped to

(12⋅τ,22⋅τ,…,ℓ∗2⋅τ).(1^{2}\cdot\tau,2^{2}\cdot\tau,\ldots,{\ell^{*}}^{2}\cdot\tau).

This is completely clear.

Definition 12.8.3.

Let ℓ≥5\ell\geq 5 be a prime number. A Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-link is an ℓ∗{\ell^{*}}-tuple

(g~1,…,g~ℓ∗)∈SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗⊂Y∞ℓ∗(\tilde{g}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{{\ell^{*}}})\in{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}\subset{Y}_{\infty}^{\ell^{*}}

lying over a tuple of elliptic curves (Eτ,1,Eτ,2,…,Eτ,ℓ∗)(E_{\tau,1},E_{\tau,2},\ldots,E_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}}) for some τ∈ℌ\tau\in\mathfrak{H} (with Eτ,jE_{\tau,j} given by the above convention and j=1,2,…,ℓ∗j=1,2,\ldots,{\ell^{*}}). The “link” here is the rule

Eτ⟼(Eτ,1,Eτ,2,…,Eτ,ℓ∗).E_{\tau}\longmapsto(E_{\tau,1},E_{\tau,2},\ldots,E_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}}).

∙\bullet

One may think of Eτ⟼(Eτ,1,Eτ,2,…,Eτ,ℓ∗)E_{\tau}\longmapsto(E_{\tau,1},E_{\tau,2},\ldots,E_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}}) as a correspondence i.e. a one-to-many function on the moduli of elliptic curves arising from the correspondence on ℌ\mathfrak{H} given by the correspondence:

τ⟼(12⋅τ,22⋅τ,…,ℓ∗2⋅τ)∈ℌℓ∗.\tau\longmapsto(1^{2}\cdot\tau,2^{2}\cdot\tau,\ldots,{\ell^{*}}^{2}\cdot\tau)\in\mathfrak{H}^{\ell^{*}}.

Theorem 12.8.5.

Let (g~1,…,g~ℓ∗)∈Y∞ℓ∗(\tilde{g}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{\ell^{*}})\in{Y}_{\infty}^{\ell^{*}} be a Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-link. Let Eτ,1,Eτ,2,…,Eτ,ℓ∗E_{\tau,1},E_{\tau,2},\ldots,E_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}} be the corresponding elliptic curves. Then

    The elliptic curves

    Eτ,1,Eτ,2,⋯,Eτ,ℓ∗E_{\tau,1},E_{\tau,2},\cdots,E_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}}

    are all isogenous to EτE_{\tau}.

    One has the tuple of the corresponding Schottky parameters

    (qτ,1,qτ,2,…,qτ,ℓ∗)∈(ℂ∗)ℓ∗(q_{\tau,1},q_{\tau,2},\ldots,q_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}})\in({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{\ell^{*}}

    corresponding to Eτ,1,Eτ,2,…,Eτ,ℓ∗E_{\tau,1},E_{\tau,2},\ldots,E_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}}.

    Let P1P_{1} correspond to the ℓ\ell-torsion point on the double cover Eτ/2E_{\tau/2} of EτE_{\tau} given by τ′=τℓ\tau^{\prime}=\frac{\tau}{\ell} and choose a Θ\Theta-function as in [Mochizuki, 2009]. Then the above tuple of Schottky parameters

    (qτ12/2​ℓ,qτ22/2​ℓ,…,qτℓ∗2/2​ℓ)∈(ℂ∗)ℓ∗(q_{\tau}^{1^{2}/2\ell},q_{\tau}^{2^{2}/2\ell},\ldots,q_{\tau}^{{\ell^{*}}^{2}/2\ell})\in({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{\ell^{*}}

Proof.

The proof is clear from the previous lemmas.

Remark 12.8.6.

Since (j001j)∈SL2​(ℚ)⊂GL2+​(ℚ)\begin{pmatrix}j&0\\ 0&\frac{1}{j}\end{pmatrix}\in{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})\subset{\rm GL}_{2}^{+}({\mathbb{Q}}), this theorem makes it clear that one can think of a Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-Link as arising from natural correspondences on the upper half plane in a manner similar to Hecke correspondences on classical modular curves. By Lemma 12.7.3, these correspondences provide a (non-trivial) scaling

qτ⟼qτj2q_{\tau}\longmapsto q_{\tau}^{j^{2}}

of the Schottky parameters. In the pp-adic case, [Joshi, 2023b] takes a similar approach via correspondences on suitable Fargues-Fontaine curves for the construction of Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-links in the context of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d]. ∙\bullet

§ 12.9 The 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-Θ\Theta-lattice

Let me note that SL2​(ℚ),SL2​(ℚ)~{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}}),\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})} are both countable sets and hence so are SL2​(ℚ)ℓ∗{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})^{\ell^{*}} and SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}. Choose an enumerating function to enumerate the elements of

SL2​(ℚ)ℓ∗={θn:n∈ℤ}.{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})^{\ell^{*}}=\{\theta_{n}:n\in{\mathbb{Z}}\}.

Then one may enumerate the set SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}} as

SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗={θn,m:(n,m)∈ℤ×ℤ},{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}=\{\theta_{n,m}:(n,m)\in{\mathbb{Z}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}\},

with the canonical surjection

SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗→SL2​(ℚ)ℓ∗{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}\to{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})^{\ell^{*}}

being given by

θn,m⟼θn.\theta_{n,m}\longmapsto\theta_{n}.

Following [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021c], one could represent the data SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗={θn,m}{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}=\{\theta_{n,m}\} as a “lattice” in the plane with the vertical direction corresponding to the fiber {θn,m:m∈ℤ}\{\theta_{n,m}:m\in{\mathbb{Z}}\} of SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗→SL2​(ℚ)ℓ∗{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}\to{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})^{\ell^{*}} over θn∈SL2​(ℚ)ℓ∗\theta_{n}\in{\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})^{\ell^{*}} i.e. over a Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-link. In this picture the fiber over θn\theta_{n} consists of 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links i.e. while the horizontal direction being represented as Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-links. In [Mochizuki, 2021c] this sort of presentation of Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-links and 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links is called the log\log-Θ\Theta-lattice:
Remark 12.9.1.

This should be compared with Mochizuki’s discussion of the log\log-Θ\Theta-lattice in [Mochizuki, 2021c, § I, Page 405] and its construction in [Mochizuki, 2021c, § 1, Page 427]. ∙\bullet

§ 12.10 Hodge structures from Schottky parametrization

This is an elaboration of [Joshi, 2020a, § 22]. Let EτE_{\tau} be an elliptic curve with period lattice [1,τ]∈ℌ[1,\tau]\in\mathfrak{H}. Then the Schottky parameterization § 12.8 provides a mixed Tate Hodge structure

HS​c​h​o​t​t​k​y​(Eτ)∈Extℤ−M​H​S1​(ℤ⁡(0),ℤ⁡(1))≃ℂ∗H_{Schottky}(E_{\tau})\in{\rm Ext}\,^{1}_{{\mathbb{Z}}-MHS}({\mathbb{Z}}(0),{\mathbb{Z}}(1))\simeq{\mathbb{C}}^{*}

given via [Deligne, 1997] by

HS​c​h​o​t​t​k​y​(Eτ)=qτ=e2​π​−1​τ∈ℂ∗.H_{Schottky}(E_{\tau})=q_{\tau}=e^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}\tau}\in{\mathbb{C}}^{*}.

This will be useful in understanding how one may carry out constructions in cohomology theory. In [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d] cohomology theory means Galois cohomology theory H1​(GLv,ℚv​(1))H^{1}(G_{L_{v}},{\mathbb{Q}}_{v}(1)) and one has

H1​(GLv,ℚv​(1))=ExtGLv1​(ℚv​(0),ℚv​(1))H^{1}(G_{L_{v}},{\mathbb{Q}}_{v}(1))={\rm Ext}\,^{1}_{G_{L_{v}}}({\mathbb{Q}}_{v}(0),{\mathbb{Q}}_{v}(1))

for each v∈𝕍Lv\in\mathbb{V}_{L}, so the analogy I make here should not be lost on the readers.

Remark 12.10.1.

Note that one way to understand the Schottky parametrization is to recognize that it asserts that the elliptic curve EτE_{\tau} is ordinary at an archimedean prime (and this ordinarity is witnessed by the Schottky Hodge structure HS​c​h​o​t​t​k​y​(Eτ)H_{Schottky}(E_{\tau})). However note that the usual Hodge structure provided by H1​(Eτ,ℤ)H^{1}(E_{\tau},{\mathbb{Z}}) is pure of weight one. Tate’s parameterization in the pp-adic context is the pp-adic version of Schottky’s paramterization. ∙\bullet

Thus one has

Lemma 12.10.2.

Any tuple (qτ,1,qτ,2,…,qτ,ℓ∗)∈(ℂ∗)ℓ∗(q_{\tau,1},q_{\tau,2},\ldots,q_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}})\in({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{\ell^{*}} in Theorem 12.8.5 provides a tuple of ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-mixed Hodge structures

(HS​c​h​o​t​t​k​y​(Eτ,1),HS​c​h​o​t​t​k​y​(Eτ,2),…,HS​c​h​o​t​t​k​y​(Eτ,ℓ∗))∈Extℤ−M​H​S1​(ℤ⁡(0),ℤ⁡(1))ℓ∗.\left(H_{Schottky}(E_{\tau,1}),H_{Schottky}(E_{\tau,2}),\ldots,H_{Schottky}(E_{\tau,{\ell^{*}}})\right)\in{\rm Ext}\,^{1}_{{\mathbb{Z}}-MHS}({\mathbb{Z}}(0),{\mathbb{Z}}(1))^{\ell^{*}}.

§ 12.11 A prelude to the definition of the Θ\Theta-values locus

Let

𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l,τ={(g~1,…,g~ℓ∗)∈SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗⊂Y∞ℓ∗:(g~1,…,g~ℓ∗)​ provides ​Eτ}.\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical,\tau}=\left\{(\tilde{g}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{\ell^{*}})\in{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}\subset{Y}_{\infty}^{\ell^{*}}:(\tilde{g}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{\ell^{*}})\text{ provides }E_{\tau}\right\}.

Let S⊂C⁡(ℂ)S\subset C({\mathbb{C}}) be the finite set of points over which the fibers of X→CX\to C are singular.

Let s∈Ss\in S be a singular point of f:X→Cf:X\to C. One would like to understand

𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l,τs\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical,\tau_{s}}

for τs∈ℌ\tau_{s}\in\mathfrak{H} in a sufficiently close i.e. in a small neighborhood of the singular point s∈Ss\in S of f:X→Cf:X\to C so that the local description of [Zhang, 2001] remains valid (for each singular point s∈Ss\in S).

§ 12.12 Mochizuki style Theta-values locus for [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000]

So to construct a Θ\Theta-values locus in the style of [Mochizuki, 2021c] one does the following. Let Y∞,s{Y}_{\infty,s} be a copy of Y∞{Y}_{\infty} indexed by an s∈Ss\in S.

Let

(12.12.1) 𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l={(g~s,1,…,g~s,ℓ∗)s∈S∈∏s∈SY∞,sℓ∗ and (g~s,1,…,g~s,ℓ∗)s∈𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l,τs for all s∈S}\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}=\left\{(\tilde{g}_{s,1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})_{s\in S}\in\prod_{s\in S}{{Y}_{\infty,s}^{\ell^{*}}}\text{ and }(\tilde{g}_{s,1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})_{s}\in\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical,\tau_{s}}\text{ for all }s\in S\right\}

Each (g~s,1,…,g~s,ℓ∗)s∈S∈𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(\tilde{g}_{s,1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})_{s\in S}\in\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical} is the analog of the Θ\Theta-pilot object, in the sense of [Mochizuki, 2021c], in the context of [Zhang, 2001, Amorós et al., 2000].

One may also define the theta-values set

𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​lv​a​l⊂Extℤ−M​H​S1​(ℤ⁡(0),ℤ⁡(1))ℓ∗,\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}^{val}\subset{\rm Ext}\,^{1}_{{\mathbb{Z}}-MHS}({\mathbb{Z}}(0),{\mathbb{Z}}(1))^{\ell^{*}},

in the style of [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c, Mochizuki, 2021d], for the context of [Zhang, 2001, Amorós et al., 2000] by taking the tuples of Schottky parameters provided by each tuple (g~s,1,…,g~s,ℓ∗)s∈S∈𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(\tilde{g}_{s,1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})_{s\in S}\in\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}.

§ 12.13 Stablized height functions hh and HH

Let

h:SL2​(ℝ)~→ℝh:\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}\to{\mathbb{R}}

be the function defined in [Zhang, 2001, Proof of Theorem 3.3] (also defined in [Amorós et al., 2000]) and denoted in [Zhang, 2001] by

ℓ:SL2​(ℝ)~→ℝ.\ell:\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}\to{\mathbb{R}}.

For g∈SL2​(ℝ)~g\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}, write

H=eh:SL2​(ℝ)~→ℝ.H=e^{h}:\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}\to{\mathbb{R}}.

One should think of hh as the logarithmic Frobenius-stabilized height function and HH as the Frobenius-stabilized height function or more simply as the stablized logarithmic height function and stablized height function respectively (also see § 12.13).

§ 12.14 Properties of the height function

The central point in the proofs of [Amorós et al., 2000, Zhang, 2001] is the following property of the height function introduced in § 12.13. By [Zhang, 2001] one has for any g~1,g~2∈SL2​(ℝ)~\tilde{g}_{1},\tilde{g}_{2}\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})}:

(12.14.1) h⁡(g~1⋅g~2)≤h⁡(g~1)+h⁡(g~2).h(\tilde{g}_{1}\cdot\tilde{g}_{2})\leq h(\tilde{g}_{1})+h(\tilde{g}_{2}).

Given a Θ\Theta-link (g~s,1,…,g~s,ℓ∗)s∈S∈𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(\tilde{g}_{s,1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})_{s\in S}\in\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}, the quantity of interest to us is:

∑s∈Sh(g~s,1⋅g~s,2⋯g~s,ℓ∗).\sum_{s\in S}h(\tilde{g}_{s,1}\cdot\tilde{g}_{s,2}\cdots\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}}).

Hence by (12.14.1) one has

∑s∈Sh(g~s,1⋅g~s,2⋯g~s,ℓ∗)≤∑s∈S∑j=1ℓ∗h(g~j).\sum_{s\in S}h(\tilde{g}_{s,1}\cdot\tilde{g}_{s,2}\cdots\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})\leq\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{j=1}^{\ell^{*}}h(\tilde{g}_{j}).

In particular one can also consider the average

1ℓ∗∑s∈Sh(g~s,1⋅g~s,2⋯g~s,ℓ∗)≤1ℓ∗∑s∈S∑j=1ℓ∗h(g~j).\frac{1}{{\ell^{*}}}\sum_{s\in S}h(\tilde{g}_{s,1}\cdot\tilde{g}_{s,2}\cdots\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})\leq\frac{1}{{\ell^{*}}}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{j=1}^{\ell^{*}}h(\tilde{g}_{j}).
Remark 12.14.2.

The proof of [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000] (and [Mochizuki, 2016]) can be understood as a sort of averaging over SL2​(ℤ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}})}. In what I do here, this averaging is being replaced here by averaging over SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}}. The innovation presented here is the idea of averaging over SL2​(ℚ)~ℓ∗{\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})}}^{\ell^{*}} which is not considered in [Mochizuki, 2016]–but corresponds to working simultaneously with Mochizuki’s Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-Links, and 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links ([Mochizuki, 2021c]). ∙\bullet

§ 12.15 The height function hh and the global Frobenius morphism (aka 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-Link)

Let me explain the reason why hh is referred to as a stabilized height function in § 12.13. Let g~τ,0′,g~τ,0∈SL2​(ℝ)~\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0},\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{R}})} and assume that

g~τ,0′=g~τ,0⋅φ∞m\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0}=\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}\cdot\varphi_{\infty}^{m}

for m∈ℤm\in{\mathbb{Z}}. By Definition 12.6.1, this equation means that g~τ,0′,g~τ,0\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0},\tilde{g}_{\tau,0} differ by an iterate of the 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-Link or equivalently differ by the mt​hm^{th} iterate of the global Frobenius φ∞\varphi_{\infty} for some m∈ℤm\in{\mathbb{Z}}. Then one has the following key relationship established in [Zhang, 2001, Proof of the Geometric Szpiro Inequality] between the heights h⁡(g~τ,0′)h(\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0}) and h⁡(g~τ,0)h(\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}) i.e. between the height of g~τ,0\tilde{g}_{\tau,0} and the height of a log-linked element g~τ,0′\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0}:

(12.15.1) h⁡(g~τ,0′)=h⁡(g~τ,0⋅φ∞m)≤h⁡(g~τ,0)+π⋅m∈ℝ.h(\tilde{g}^{\prime}_{\tau,0})=h(\tilde{g}_{\tau,0}\cdot\varphi_{\infty}^{m})\leq h(\tilde{g}_{\tau,0})+\pi\cdot m\in{\mathbb{R}}.

(where π∈ℝ\pi\in{\mathbb{R}} is the familiar real number).

This property plays a central role in the proof of [Zhang, 2001, Proof of the Geometric Szpiro Inequality] and Mochizuki’s discussion of this point and its relationship to his proof can be found in [Mochizuki, 2016].

§ 12.16 The definition of |𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l​(D)|\left|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right|

More generally, keeping in mind [Mochizuki, 2021d], let S⊂D⊂C⁡(ℂ)S\subset D\subset C({\mathbb{C}}) be a subset containing SS such that the local theory of [Zhang, 2001] can be applied (for example let DD be the disjoint union of small disk Ds⊂C⁡(ℂ)D_{s}\subset C({\mathbb{C}}) around each s∈Ss\in S). Then it is possible to define 𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l​(D)⊃𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\supset\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical} as follows:

Definition 12.16.1.

For a compact domain S⊂D⊂C⁡(ℂ)S\subset D\subset C({\mathbb{C}}) chosen as above, let

|𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(D)|=sup{∑s∈S∑j=1ℓ∗h(g~s,j):(g~s,1,g~2⋯,g~s,ℓ∗)s∈S∈𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(D)}.\left|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right|=\sup\left\{\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{j=1}^{\ell^{*}}h(\tilde{g}_{s,j}):(\tilde{g}_{s,1},\tilde{g}_{2}\cdots,\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})_{s\in S}\in\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right\}.

∙\bullet

The following lemma will be useful:

Lemma 12.16.2.
|𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(D)|≥sup{∑s∈Sh(g~s,1⋅g~2⋯g~s,ℓ∗):(g~s,1,g~2⋯,g~s,ℓ∗)s∈S∈𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(D)}\left|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right|\geq\sup\left\{\sum_{s\in S}h(\tilde{g}_{s,1}\cdot\tilde{g}_{2}\cdots\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}}):(\tilde{g}_{s,1},\tilde{g}_{2}\cdots,\tilde{g}_{s,{\ell^{*}}})_{s\in S}\in\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right\}

Proof.

This is immediate from the above discussed property (12.14.1) of hh and the definition of |𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l​(D)|\left|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right|.

Remark 12.16.3.

Working with a compact domain DD is analogous to working with compactly bounded domains (in the sense of [Mochizuki, 2010]) in the proof of the main theorem of [Mochizuki, 2021d]. ∙\bullet

§ 12.17 The monodromy representation and its reduction modulo ℓ\ell

Let π1t​o​p​(C⁡(ℂ)−S,∗)\pi_{1}^{top}(C({\mathbb{C}})-S,*) be the topological fundamental group of C⁡(ℂ)−SC({\mathbb{C}})-S for some choice of basepoint ∗∈C⁡(ℂ)−S*\in C({\mathbb{C}})-S. This is a group with 2​g+|S|2g+\left|S\right| generators

a1,…,b1,…,ag,bg,{γs}s∈Sa_{1},\ldots,b_{1},\ldots,a_{g},b_{g},\{\gamma_{s}\}_{s\in S}

and one relation

∏j=1g[aj,bj]​∏s∈Sγs=1\prod_{j=1}^{g}[a_{j},b_{j}]\prod_{s\in S}\gamma_{s}=1

between these generators.

Let t∈C⁡(ℂ)−St\in C({\mathbb{C}})-S be a general point and XtX_{t} be the fiber of X→C⁡(ℂ)X\to C({\mathbb{C}}) over this point and consider the monodromy representation (on the singular homology)

ρ:π1t​o​p​(C⁡(ℂ)−S,∗)→A​u​t​(H1​(Xt,ℤ)),\rho:\pi_{1}^{top}(C({\mathbb{C}})-S,*)\to{Aut}(H_{1}(X_{t},{\mathbb{Z}})),

and also its “reduction modulo ℓ\ell”:

ρℓ:π1t​o​p​(C⁡(ℂ)−S,∗)→A​u​t​(H1​(Xt,ℤ/ℓ)).\rho_{\ell}:\pi_{1}^{top}(C({\mathbb{C}})-S,*)\to{Aut}(H_{1}(X_{t},{\mathbb{Z}}/\ell)).

One can assume without any loss of generality that ρℓ\rho_{\ell} is irreducible otherwise by a classical argument due to Faltings, Szpiro’s inequality is trivial.

At any point s∈Ss\in S one has the monodromy around ss which is the image of ρ⁡(γs)\rho(\gamma_{s}) and also ρℓ​(γs)\rho_{\ell}(\gamma_{s}). Let γ~s(j)∈SL2​(ℤ)~\tilde{\gamma}^{(j)}_{s}\in\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}})} be an arbitrary lift of ρℓ​(γsj2)\rho_{\ell}(\gamma_{s}^{j^{2}}) for j=1,…,ℓ∗j=1,\ldots,{\ell^{*}}.

§ 12.18 Mochizuki’s Corollary 3.12 in the geometric case

[Mochizuki, 2021c, Corollary 3.12] now has a simple formulation with a tautological proof:

Theorem 12.18.1.

For a compact domain DD as above, and any choice of (g~1,…,g~ℓ∗)∈𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l​(D)(\tilde{g}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{\ell^{*}})\in\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D) , one has

|𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l(D)|≥∑s∈S∑j=1ℓ∗h(γ~s(j))≥h(∏s∈Sγ~s(1)⋅γ~s(2)⋯γ~s(ℓ∗)).\left|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right|\geq\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{j=1}^{\ell^{*}}h(\tilde{\gamma}_{s}^{(j)})\geq h\left(\prod_{s\in S}\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}_{s}\cdot\tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}_{s}\cdots\tilde{\gamma}^{({\ell^{*}})}_{s}\right).

Proof.

The lower bound is immediate from Lemma 12.16.2 and the fact that, by Definition 12.16.1, |𝚯c​l​a​s​s​i​c​a​l​(D)|\left|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{classical}(D)\right| is the supremum of all such sums.

Remark 12.18.2.

One can think of the product ∏s∈S(γ~s(1)⋅γ~s(2)⋯γ~s(ℓ∗))\prod_{s\in S}\left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}_{s}\cdot\tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}_{s}\cdots\tilde{\gamma}^{({\ell^{*}})}_{s}\right) and more generally the product ∏s∈S(γ~s(1)⋅γ~s(2)⋯γ~s(ℓ))\prod_{s\in S}\left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}_{s}\cdot\tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}_{s}\cdots\tilde{\gamma}^{(\ell)}_{s}\right) as a “simulation” of a “multiplicative” one dimensional subspace of ρℓ\rho_{\ell}. Since ρℓ\rho_{\ell} is irreducible there does not exist any natural one dimensional subspace (globally) in ρℓ\rho_{\ell}. This multiplicative subspace point of view is due to [Mochizuki, 2021c]. ∙\bullet

§ 12.19 Additional Remarks

At this point I want to make the following important remarks.

  1. (1)

    Working with SL2​(ℚ)⊂GL2+​(ℚ){\rm SL_{2}}({\mathbb{Q}})\subset{\rm GL}_{2}^{+}({\mathbb{Q}}) is essentially equivalent to Mochizuki’s idea of working with Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-links and working with φ∞\varphi_{\infty} is equivalent 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links (in [Joshi, 2023b], I prove both these assertions in the pp-adic context).

  2. (2)

    Especially working with SL2​(ℚ)~\widetilde{{\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}})} allows us to work with Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-links and 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-links simultaneously. In [Mochizuki, 2021a, Mochizuki, 2021b, Mochizuki, 2021c], Mochizuki works with Θg​a​u\Theta_{gau}-Links and 𝔩​𝔬​𝔤\mathfrak{log}-Links separately. My construction of Mochizuki’s Ansatz in [Joshi, 2023b] allows me to work with both these devices simultaneously.

  3. (3)

    The global Frobenius morphism (12.5.1) plays a central role in [Zhang, 2001], [Amorós et al., 2000].

  4. (4)

    The global relation between generators of the topological fundamental group

    π1t​o​p​(C⁡(ℂ)−S,∗),\pi_{1}^{top}(C({\mathbb{C}})-S,*),

    namely

    ∏j=1g[ai,bi]​∏s∈Sγs=1,\prod_{j=1}^{g}[a_{i},b_{i}]\prod_{s\in S}\gamma_{s}=1,

    plays the role of the product formula (2.1.1) in the theory of arithmeticoids and their height functions.

  5. (5)

    The function hh, which is denoted by ℓ\ell in [Zhang, 2001], plays the role of stabilized height function in the proof of the geometric Szpiro Inequality in [Zhang, 2001].

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
